s01.headline: I was at Jantar Mantar 1.0.
s01.headline2: If you’re going for 2.0, here’s what I want you to know.
s01.deck: What has actually been happening, how to look after yourself and the person next to you, and how to keep proof nobody can take from you.

s02.headline: Before you leave, know what’s changed.
s02.foot: Police have refused permission and prohibitory orders are in force. If you’re going, go knowing that.

s03.headline: Don’t plan for the rules. Plan for what’s been happening.
s03.lede: All of this was reported in the past few weeks, at Jantar Mantar or a few streets away. Police deny some of it. Plan as though any of it could happen to you.
items: No name tags
On 2 Oct journalists asked officers why they weren’t wearing name tags. Nobody would say.
The Wire, 5 Oct
Women taken away alone, after dark
A student leader says she was put in a private-looking car with no woman officer and driven to Narela.
The Wire, The Quint, 5–6 Oct
Hands on women
Three women journalists say officers touched them. One names an ACP. Another says her shirt was lifted inside a bus.
The Wire, The Quint, ABC
No video, no FIR
The women who complained were told an FIR would come only if someone produced video.
The Quint, 6 Oct
Cameras go first
Reporters lost cameras, mics, phones, even glasses, in the minutes before they were pushed into buses.
The Quint, 6 Oct
Batons and tear gas
Both were used on 20 July. By the police’s own count, about 60 protesters were hurt.
NPR, TIME, July

s04.headline: Your phone may stop working. Get ready before it does.
s04.testimony: At Jantar Mantar 1.0 in July, I couldn’t reach people for long stretches, and 112 was no use to me.
s04.confirmed: Mobile internet is reported off within about 4 km of Jantar Mantar until 10 pm on 10 Oct.
s04.unverified: Talk of calls being jammed hasn’t been verified. Plan as if it might happen anyway.
steps: Download this guide now, while you still have signal.
Write two numbers on your arm in marker: someone at home, and a lawyer.
Switch off face and fingerprint unlock. Use a PIN.
Tell your family you might go quiet for hours, and that silence doesn’t mean the worst.
Pick a time and a place to find each other if you get separated.
Carry cash. UPI and cab apps won’t work without data.
Work out tonight how you’d get home without an app.

s05.headline: Pack for the day going wrong.
items: Water
More than you think you’ll need
Food and ORS
Something that won’t spoil in a bag
Your medicines
With a note of any condition you have
Power bank
Charged tonight
Phone with a PIN
Face and fingerprint unlock off
Marker pen
For numbers on your arm, and notes
Cash
Enough to get home from the edge of the city
One ID
Nothing more than you need
Shoes you can move in
You may walk far, or fast
Spare glasses
Reporters lost theirs in the pushing
Whatever your body needs
Mobility aids, personal care, sanitary supplies
s05.note: Leave at home anything you’d hate to lose. Don’t leave behind anything your body needs.

s06.headline: Don’t be alone there. Not for a minute.
body: Go with at least one person. Know their full name, someone to call at home, and any medical condition they have.

Decide tonight what happens if one of you is taken. The other notes the time, the place, the vehicle number and which way it turned, shouts the name loud enough for others to hear, and starts calling.
If you see a woman being pulled away on her own, stay. Film it, call out her name if you know it, and get a number to her somehow.
s06.boundary_label: Be warm with strangers. Don’t be trusting.
s06.boundary: Nobody is owed your number or your company, and nobody, in uniform or not, should be leading you somewhere alone.
s06.close: By evening, the stranger next to you may be the only person who saw what happened to you.

s07.kicker: 07 · If someone puts their hands on you
s07.headline: If someone puts their hands on you, make noise.
s07.sub: Even if it’s a police officer. Especially then.
steps: Say exactly what’s happening
Loudly, in plain words. “He’s touching me.” “Where’s the woman officer?” People turn, and phones come out.
Get it on someone’s phone
Ask whoever is nearest to film. Afterwards, take their name and number. You’ll need them.
Find out who it is
Name tag, rank, helmet number, the van’s number. If there’s no name tag, say so out loud while someone is filming.
Ask for a woman officer, on camera
Women are meant to be searched only by women, and not arrested after sunset except in exceptional cases. Saying it won’t stop them. It puts it on record. BNSS s. 49, 43(5)
Don’t swing back
Any push you return becomes their excuse, and a case against you. Keep your hands where the camera can see them.
s07.after: None of this is your fault. Tell someone tonight, and see slide 10 for keeping the record.

s08.headline: If they put you in a bus.
steps: Shout your name and a number
Your full name and a number at home, as you’re being taken. Someone outside will remember it.
Use the window
On 4 Oct a reporter wrote what was being done to her, and a phone number, on a scrap of paper and pressed it to the glass for her friends outside.
Ask where they’re taking you
“Kis thane le ja rahe ho?” Then repeat the answer out loud to everyone on the bus.
Say your medical condition at once
Diabetes, asthma, pregnancy, anything. Say it to the officers and to the people around you.
Keep your phone locked
If they take it, don’t unlock it for them.
Don’t get split off
Stay with the group. If they try to put you alone in an unmarked car, make noise and ask for a woman officer.
s08.expect: Most people picked up in recent weeks were held for a few hours at a police station or a stadium and let go in the evening, sometimes on the far edge of the city. That’s what the cash in your pocket is for.
s08.outside: Find out which police station. Go there with a couple of others, and call their family and a lawyer. Don’t post their phone number or address.

s09.headline: They go for cameras first. Record anyway.

cols.label: Record
items: Film from a distance, in short clips.
Get faces, helmet and van numbers, and name tags or the lack of them.
Keep filming before and after, not only the worst moment.
Say the date, time and place out loud.

cols.label: Keep it safe
items: Hand clips to a friend away from the front.
Keep the original file, with sound. Don’t trim or filter it.
Copy it somewhere else the moment you get signal.

cols.label: Before you post
items: Blur anyone who could be hurt for being seen.
If it’s evidence, show a lawyer first.

s09.impersonation: The women who complained on 3 Oct were told there’d be no FIR without video. Your clip may be the only thing that backs someone up.
s09.close: Footage that exists in three places is hard to make disappear.

s10.headline: Nobody official is coming to fix this. Build the record yourself.
steps: Write it all down tonight
Times, places, any names or numbers you saw, the exact words used, who was standing nearby. Memory goes fast.
Show your injuries to a doctor
One you trust. Keep the report, and photograph every bruise with the date visible.
Copy your footage to three places
Your phone, a friend’s phone, and somewhere online once you have signal. Never edit the original.
Take it to an independent lawyer
HRLN, APCR, PUCL, or a lawyer you know. They’ll tell you what’s worth pursuing, and how.
Give it to journalists you trust
Independent reporters and fact-checkers, the ones who were actually there. Keep your original.
Check on people the next day
Including the ones who say they’re fine.
s10.note: When anything has moved after a protest, it was usually because there was footage, there were witnesses, and somebody refused to let it drop.

s11.headline: Numbers to have on paper.
s11.honest: The organisers set up a legal-aid fund and volunteer lawyers in July. Get their legal contact from their official handle before you leave. I couldn’t confirm any lawyer or doctor on the ground for tomorrow.

s12.headline: I hope everyone gets home safe.
s12.body: You’ll be angry tomorrow, and you’ll have every right to be. Shout. Just don’t be on your own, and don’t hand them the excuse they’re waiting for. Film what you can. If something happens to you or to the person beside you, it doesn’t end when the bus doors open. Write it down, show a doctor, copy the footage, find a lawyer, and keep at it until somebody answers for it.

1.headline: I was at Jantar Mantar 1.0 in July.
1.body: If you’re going for 2.0 tomorrow, this is what I’d want you to have read first: what has actually been happening, what to do if someone grabs you or puts you in a bus, and how to keep proof nobody can take from you.
1.cta: Full guide on my profile. Save it while you have signal.

2.headline: Do these tonight.
items: Write a home number and a lawyer’s on your arm.
Turn off face unlock. Use a PIN.
Pair up. Swap full names and numbers.
Pick a time and place to regroup.
Pack cash, water, medicines, spare glasses.
Tell family you may go quiet for hours.
